c-em-01-q046.boardCall: Dislocated knee + absent distal pulses + ischemic limb -> immediate closed reduction of knee
c-em-01-q046.hinge: Acute knee dislocation with limb ischemia (absent distal pulses) mandates immediate closed reduction to relieve popliteal neurovascular traction before imaging.
c-em-01-q046.trap: CT arteriography is crucial to assess popliteal artery injury, but waiting for angiography before reducing the joint causes prolonged ischemia and limb loss.

A.clue: Doppler systolic pressure ratio screening vascular injury
A.fit: Not here: gross joint dislocation with absent pulses requires immediate joint reduction first

B.clue: Ultrasonographic evaluation of deep venous thrombosis
B.fit: Not here: acute arterial occlusion and joint dislocation, not venous thrombosis

C.clue: Electrophysiological testing of peripheral nerve conduction
C.fit: Not here: acute trauma emergency requiring immediate joint relocation
C.tempting: absent sensation from knee to toes

D.clue: Radiographic contrast imaging of lower extremity veins
D.fit: Not here: inappropriate for acute knee dislocation and arterial ischemia

E.clue: Immediate closed manual relocation of tibiofemoral joint
E.fit: Here: knee dislocation with absent distal pulses, anesthesia, and motor loss

F.clue: Invasive fluoroscopic contrast imaging of popliteal artery
F.fit: Not here: imaging prior to joint reduction delays critical reperfusion and worsens ischemia
F.tempting: popliteal artery injury is extremely common

algorithm.title: Acute knee dislocation and popliteal vascular injury

nodes.text: Recognize acute knee dislocation (tibiofemoral disruption) with high risk of popliteal artery transection
Perform immediate closed reduction with longitudinal traction under conscious sedation
Re-examine neurovascular status immediately after reduction: palpate DP/PT pulses
**Asymmetrical pulses, absent pulses, or hard vascular signs post-reduction:** emergent surgical exploration in operating room
**Normal symmetric palpable pulses post-reduction:** measure ankle-brachial index (ABI)
**ABI < 0.90:** perform urgent CT angiography of the lower extremity
**ABI >= 0.90:** perform serial vascular examinations every 2-4 hours for 24 hours
Immobilize knee in 15-20 degrees of flexion with posterior long-leg splint

triggers.text: discoloration and a dislocated knee
Sensation is absent from the knee to the toes.
No motor activity is present.
There are no palpable pulses distal to the femoral artery.

c-em-01-q047.boardCall: New-onset type 1 diabetes + polydipsia + Kussmaul respirations 28/min + dehydration -> decreased serum bicarbonate (DKA)
c-em-01-q047.hinge: New-onset diabetic ketoacidosis produces severe ketoacid accumulation with high anion gap metabolic acidosis, marked by decreased serum bicarbonate.
c-em-01-q047.trap: Total body potassium and phosphate are depleted, but extracellular shifts often keep their initial serum concentrations normal or elevated.

A.clue: Depleted buffer base in high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis
A.fit: Here: polydipsia, tachypnea 28/min, dry mucosa, and dehydration from ketoacidosis

B.clue: Reduced serum extracellular inorganic phosphorus concentration
B.fit: Not here: transcellular shift from insulin lack maintains normal or elevated early serum phosphate
B.tempting: total body phosphate is depleted in DKA

C.clue: Low extracellular serum potassium concentration
C.fit: Not here: acidemia and insulin deficiency shift potassium extracellularly, keeping serum levels normal or high

D.clue: Elevated extracellular alkali buffer concentration
D.fit: Not here: severe ketoacidosis consumes bicarbonate rather than elevating it

E.clue: Elevated serum inorganic phosphorus concentration
E.fit: Not here: ketoacidosis universally depresses bicarbonate, which is the defining diagnostic criterion
E.tempting: acidosis drives phosphate out of cells

F.fit: Not here: metabolic ketoacid consumption makes decreased bicarbonate the defining abnormality
F.tempting: insulin deficiency causes extracellular potassium shift

nodes.text: DKA ketoacids consume bicarbonate, producing high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis.
Confirm ketonemia with pH <7.3 or bicarbonate <18 and glucose ≥200 mg/dL or known diabetes.
Begin IV isotonic crystalloid and check potassium.
**Potassium <3.5 mEq/L:** replace potassium and delay insulin.
**Potassium ≥3.5 mEq/L:** start IV regular insulin.
**Glucose <250 mg/dL:** add dextrose while continuing insulin.
Continue until ketones <0.6 mmol/L and pH ≥7.3 or bicarbonate ≥18.

triggers.text: reports being very thirsty recently
respirations are 28/min
dry mucous membranes
feeling light-headed upon standing and says she almost fainted earlier today

c-em-01-q048.boardCall: Marathon runner in humid heat + core temperature 40.5°C + obtundation + hypotension -> exertional heat stroke
c-em-01-q048.hinge: Severe hyperthermia (temperature > 40°C) accompanied by central nervous system dysfunction (obtundation) after exertion defines heat stroke.
c-em-01-q048.trap: Rhabdomyolysis with elevated CK is a common complication, but profound encephalopathy and core temp 40.5°C make heat stroke the overarching diagnosis.

A.clue: Synthetic androgen excess causing cardiac and psychiatric toxicity
A.fit: Not here: acute exertional hyperthermia with core temperature 40.5°C

B.clue: Core temperature > 40°C with CNS impairment
B.fit: Here: temperature 40.5°C, obtundation, shock, and end-organ dysfunction after 26-mile run

C.clue: Dopamine D2 antagonist reaction with lead-pipe rigidity
C.fit: Not here: no exposure to neuroleptic agents and no lead-pipe muscular rigidity

D.clue: Skeletal muscle breakdown releasing myoglobin into circulation
D.fit: Not here: rhabdomyolysis alone does not account for acute coma and core temperature 40.5°C

E.clue: Infection-induced dysregulated host response and septic shock
E.fit: Not here: acute collapse during warm-weather marathon without antecedent bacterial infection

algorithm.title: Exertional heat stroke evaluation and management

nodes.text: Hyperthermia with CNS dysfunction after exertion indicates heat stroke.
Begin cold-water immersion immediately and monitor rectal temperature; stop active cooling near 39°C.
**Hypotension or hypovolemia:** IV isotonic crystalloid concurrently with cooling; reassess perfusion.
**Shivering or seizures:** IV lorazepam or diazepam.
Monitor CK, renal function, electrolytes, liver enzymes, and coagulation for evolving organ injury.
Avoid antipyretics; they do not correct environmental hyperthermia.

triggers.text: collapsing near the completion of a 26-mile run in warm, humid weather
temperature is 40.5°C (104.9°F)
obtunded and warm
Creatine kinase 1000 U/L

c-em-01-q049.boardCall: Weight loss + heat intolerance + multinodular goiter + tachycardia 130/min + fever 38.5°C -> oral or IV propranolol
c-em-01-q049.hinge: Acute thyrotoxicosis with severe beta-adrenergic symptoms (tachycardia, diaphoresis, hyperthermia) is treated first-line with propranolol.
c-em-01-q049.trap: Iodine blocks thyroid hormone release, but giving it before a thionamide provides substrate for new hormone synthesis and worsens storm.

A.clue: Divalent cation mineral for acute symptomatic hypocalcemia
A.fit: Not here: does not blunt beta-adrenergic hyperactivity or hyperthyroidism

B.clue: Inorganic iodide solution blocking thyroid hormone release
B.fit: Not here: administration before thionamide provides substrate and worsens thyrotoxicosis

C.clue: Systemic glucocorticoid reducing peripheral T4 to T3 conversion
C.fit: Not here: secondary adjunctive therapy that follows immediate beta-adrenergic blockade

D.clue: Nonselective beta-adrenergic blocker blunting sympathetic hyperactivity
D.fit: Here: heart palpitations, pulse 130/min, diaphoresis, and fever 38.5°C with goiter

E.clue: Synthetic levothyroxine hormone replacement
E.fit: Not here: contraindicated because excess thyroid hormone is the causative agent

nodes.text: Fever, tachycardia, diaphoresis, delirium, goiter: acute thyrotoxicosis / thyroid storm
Immediate oral or IV propranolol
**Asthma or decompensated HF contraindicating β-blockers:** diltiazem for rate control
Propylthiouracil or methimazole to block new hormone synthesis
**≥ 1 hour after thionamide:** potassium iodide (SSKI) or Lugol solution
IV hydrocortisone to block peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion
Active cooling + acetaminophen; avoid aspirin (displaces T4 from TBG)

triggers.text: 3 hours after the onset of heart palpitations
pulse is 130/min
always feeling warm
A photograph of the neck is shown.
temperature is 38.5°C (101.3°F)

c-em-01-q050.boardCall: Severe hypoglycemia (15 mg/dL) + unresponsiveness + no IV access -> intramuscular glucagon
c-em-01-q050.hinge: Severe hypoglycemia with neuroglycopenia and impossible IV access requires immediate intramuscular glucagon to stimulate hepatic glycogenolysis.
c-em-01-q050.trap: Oral glucose or hard candies are strictly contraindicated in obtunded patients due to high aspiration risk.

A.clue: Passive external rewarming device for hypothermia
A.fit: Not here: hypothermia is secondary to neuroglycopenia and resolves once glucose is restored

B.clue: Manual positive-pressure ventilation via mask
B.fit: Not here: oxygen saturation is 96% and hypoventilation resolves upon reversing hypoglycemia

C.clue: Hepatic glycogenolytic peptide promoting glucose release
C.fit: Here: fingerstick glucose 15 mg/dL with unresponsiveness and no intravenous access

D.clue: Oral fast-acting simple carbohydrate ingestion
D.fit: Not here: uncooperative moaning patient has lost airway protective reflexes with aspiration risk

E.clue: Rectal mucosal installation of hypertonic glucose
E.fit: Not here: unpredictable and slow absorption compared to intramuscular glucagon

nodes.text: Recognize severe hypoglycemia: blood glucose < 54 mg/dL with neuroglycopenia or altered consciousness
**Patient conscious and able to swallow:** administer oral fast-acting carbohydrates
**Unconscious or impaired consciousness with IV access:** administer IV dextrose
**Unconscious or impaired consciousness without IV access:** administer intramuscular glucagon
Recheck fingerstick glucose every 15 minutes until blood glucose > 70 mg/dL
**Sulfonylurea-induced prolonged hypoglycemia (glimepiride):** administer subcutaneous octreotide
Admit for prolonged observation due to extended duration of sulfonylurea action

The nurses continue to have difficulty obtaining intravenous access.
His medications are glimepiride and metformin.
patient is diaphoretic and moaning softly
temperature is 34.8°C (94.6°F)

abdominal-trauma.name: Abdominal trauma
abdominal-trauma.scope: Blunt abdominal trauma (splenic/hepatic laceration, FAST exam, CT scan), penetrating abdominal trauma (stab, gunshot, peritonitis, exploratory laparotomy indications)
abdominal-trauma.core: Abdominal injury after collision, fall, stabbing, or gunshot: hemodynamic status and peritoneal signs determine imaging versus immediate operation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: High-speed deceleration, seat-belt compression, lower rib fractures; anticoagulation increases bleeding risk
Stab wounds may spare viscera; bullets frequently injure multiple structures

rows.label: Clues
items: LUQ pain or referred left shoulder pain → splenic injury; RUQ tenderness → hepatic injury
Distention, ecchymoses, abdominal wall marks; initially benign examination does not exclude bowel injury
★ **Rigidity, rebound, persistent hypotension**, or evisceration → urgent operative assessment

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Solid-organ disruption → intraperitoneal hemorrhage; mesenteric injury → ischemia or delayed perforation
Retroperitoneal injury may produce little intraperitoneal free fluid

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **FAST** at bedside during resuscitation; detects free fluid, not organ-specific injury
★ Stable → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast**; evaluate solid organs, bowel, retroperitoneum
Negative FAST with ongoing shock → search thorax/pelvis, repeat assessment; do not assume safety
Stable anterior stab → local wound exploration or serial examination/CT; trajectory guides evaluation

rows.label: Tx
items: Airway, large-bore IV access, warmed blood products; massive transfusion for hemorrhagic shock
★ Unstable + positive FAST, peritonitis, or ongoing transfusion need → **exploratory laparotomy**; no CT delay
Stable splenic/hepatic injury → monitored nonoperative care; blush, transient response → angioembolization (older questions: laparotomy)
Enteric contents, uncontrolled bleeding → operation; transperitoneal gunshot → **laparotomy** even if stable; selected stabs observed
Suspected bowel perforation → ceftriaxone + metronidazole, trauma surgery; free subdiaphragmatic air → **laparotomy**, no CT

rows.label: Complications
items: Delayed splenic rupture, abscess, bile leak, abdominal compartment syndrome
Missed hollow-viscus injury → sepsis; splenectomy → overwhelming encapsulated bacterial infection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Restraints, airbags, injury-prevention counseling
★ After splenectomy → **pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib vaccines**; fever requires urgent antibiotics

rows.label: Mimics
items: Pelvic hemorrhage: unstable pelvis, negative abdominal FAST
Tension pneumothorax: unilateral absent breath sounds, obstructive shock

abdominal-trauma.evidence: Not checked online; established trauma assessment and management principles.

acute-coronary-syndromes.name: Acute coronary syndromes
acute-coronary-syndromes.scope: Unstable angina, NSTEMI, STEMI, cardiac biomarkers, risk stratification (HEART/TIMI), antiplatelet and anticoagulation, reperfusion
acute-coronary-syndromes.core: Acute myocardial ischemia from coronary plaque disruption: distinguish occlusive infarction needing immediate reperfusion from non-ST-elevation syndromes needing risk-guided invasive management.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Smoking, diabetes, hypertension, dyslipidemia, CKD, age, premature family CAD
Cocaine/stimulants, anemia, tachyarrhythmia may provoke ischemia; distinguish supply-demand injury from plaque rupture

rows.label: Clues
items: Pressure with arm/jaw radiation, diaphoresis, nausea; older adults/diabetes may have dyspnea or epigastric pain alone
Inferior MI with hypotension, clear lungs, raised JVP → suspect RV infarction
★ New murmur, pulmonary edema, shock after MI → **mechanical complication**, urgent echo
Unexplained crash/syncope + ischemic ECG → primary MI; troponin over trauma imaging

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Platelet activation and thrombin-mediated clot reduce coronary perfusion; necrosis releases troponin
Type 2 MI: oxygen mismatch without acute atherothrombosis; treat precipitating cause

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **ECG within 10 minutes**, repeat if nondiagnostic; serial high-sensitivity troponin using validated pathway
Posterior suspicion → V7–V9; inferior MI → right-sided leads; new LBBB alone insufficient for STEMI
★ **Do not wait for troponin before STEMI reperfusion**; bedside echo if diagnosis/complications uncertain
HEART ≤3 + negative serial troponins → low risk; TIMI/GRACE stratifies NSTE-ACS
STE: **V1–V6 → LAD**; **II, III, aVF + bradycardia → RCA**; I, aVL → circumflex

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Chewed aspirin**, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulant such as heparin, high-intensity atorvastatin; oxygen only if hypoxemic
Nitroglycerin (**venodilation** → ↓preload) for pain unless hypotension, RV infarction, recent PDE5 inhibitor; avoid NSAIDs
★ STEMI → **primary PCI** within 90 minutes at PCI center, ≤120 minutes including transfer
IF PCI delay >120 minutes, symptoms <12 hours, no contraindication → fibrinolysis promptly, then transfer

rows.label: Complications
items: VT/VF, AV block, HF, cardiogenic shock; free-wall rupture
Later aneurysm/thrombus, embolism, Dressler syndrome; antithrombotics → bleeding
Post-MI murmur: **papillary rupture** → apical, no O₂ step-up; **septal rupture** → left sternal, RA→RV step-up

rows.label: Prevention
items: DAPT usually 12 months after ACS unless bleeding risk changes plan; cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation
ACE inhibitor/ARB for LV dysfunction; beta-blocker when stable, avoid in shock or acute decompensation

rows.label: Mimics
items: Aortic dissection: abrupt tearing pain/pulse deficit; anticoagulation or lysis dangerous
Pericarditis: positional pleuritic pain, diffuse changes
PE: hypoxemia, thrombotic risk, RV strain

table.title: Syndrome branches
rows: Urgent catheterization if unstable; otherwise risk-guided angiography
Regional ST elevation or occlusion equivalent
Prior intracranial hemorrhage, active bleeding, suspected dissection
Stress or perfusion testing within 72 hours

alcohol-withdrawal.name: Alcohol withdrawal
alcohol-withdrawal.core: Autonomic and neuropsychiatric excitation after reducing prolonged heavy alcohol intake; progression from mild symptoms to life-threatening delirium.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior withdrawal seizures/delirium, repeated detoxifications, heavy sustained use, older age
Acute illness, electrolyte depletion, concurrent sedative dependence; poor support increases outpatient failure

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ Diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, insomnia, nausea; symptoms possible with **positive blood alcohol**
Hospital day 2–5 or postoperative: new agitation, hallucinations, autonomic signs → suspect **unreported alcohol use**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Chronic ethanol → downregulated GABA inhibition/upregulated NMDA excitation; cessation unmasks neuronal hyperactivity
Repeated episodes → kindling, progressively lower seizure threshold

rows.label: Dx
items: **Clinical diagnosis** + time since reduction; bedside glucose, CBC, electrolytes, Mg, phosphate, liver tests
★ **CIWA-Ar** if communicative; ≥19 severe; delirium/intubation → **RASS/MINDS**
First/focal seizure, head injury, focal deficit, atypical timing → head CT; do not assume withdrawal

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Diazepam/chlordiazepoxide** symptom-triggered; liver dysfunction/older frail adults → **lorazepam/oxazepam**
★ Seizures/delirium → monitored inpatient **IV benzodiazepines**; refractory → ICU phenobarbital with respiratory monitoring
★ **Parenteral thiamine**; hypoglycemia → immediate dextrose, never wait; correct electrolyte deficits
Phenytoin ineffective; dexmedetomidine adjunct; **chlorpromazine**/antipsychotics lower seizure threshold, prolong QT

rows.label: Complications
items: Aspiration, dysrhythmias, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis; excessive sedation → respiratory depression
Malnutrition → Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia; suspected → high-dose IV thiamine
Pregnancy: seizures, adrenergic surge → fetal hypoxia; **maternal withdrawal** is greatest immediate fetal risk

rows.label: Prevention
items: High-risk inpatients → preventive benzodiazepines; outpatient withdrawal only if mild, reliable supervision
Recovery: **naltrexone** unless opioids/acute hepatitis; **acamprosate** unless severe CKD; addiction follow-up

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatic encephalopathy: asterixis, decompensated cirrhosis, less autonomic excitation
Sepsis: infectious source, hypotension, persistent inflammatory findings
Sedative withdrawal: benzodiazepine/barbiturate reduction; similar syndrome, different exposure
Anticholinergic delirium: dry skin, urinary retention; diaphoresis favors withdrawal

table.title: Approximate onset after reduction; overlap common
rows: Visual/auditory/tactile hallucinations; clear sensorium; vitals near normal
Disorientation, hallucinations, fever, tremor, marked autonomic instability

anaphylaxis.name: Anaphylaxis
anaphylaxis.scope: Anaphylaxis, angioedema, biphasic reactions, epinephrine autoinjector, emergency airway management
anaphylaxis.core: Rapid multisystem reaction after exposure—or isolated hypotension or airway compromise after a known allergen—requires epinephrine immediately.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Foods, insect venom, antibiotics, latex; exercise can amplify food-triggered reactions
Asthma, prior severe reaction, mast-cell disorders; beta-blockers can complicate treatment

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Urticaria/angioedema + wheeze, stridor, hypotension, or severe GI symptoms**
Skin findings may be absent; hoarseness and tongue swelling predict airway danger
Biphasic recurrence after apparent resolution, especially after severe or undertreated episodes

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mast-cell/basophil mediators → vasodilation, capillary leak, bronchoconstriction; often IgE-mediated
Epinephrine: α1 reverses vasodilation/edema, β2 reverses bronchoconstriction; albuterol alone misses edema and shock

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical diagnosis**; never wait for tryptase or laboratory confirmation
Acute and baseline serum tryptase can support uncertain cases; normal results do not exclude anaphylaxis

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg**, adult 0.3–0.5 mg, lateral thigh; repeat every 5–15 minutes
Supine with legs elevated unless respiratory distress; oxygen, early intubation for progressive obstruction
Profound shock or refractory hypotension → titrated IV epinephrine plus **isotonic boluses**; beta-blocker use → glucagon
Albuterol for residual bronchospasm; antihistamines relieve itching only; steroids do not reliably prevent biphasic reactions
★ Monitor until resolved; **longer observation/admission** after hypotension, repeated epinephrine, or severe asthma

rows.label: Complications
items: Asphyxia, distributive shock, arrhythmia, hypoxic brain injury
Undiluted IV epinephrine bolus errors → ischemia and dangerous dysrhythmia

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Prescribe **epinephrine autoinjector**, demonstrate technique, provide written action plan and allergy referral
Extra device for repeat-dose risk; avoidance, medical alert ID; venom immunotherapy after qualifying sting allergy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Vasovagal episode: bradycardia, pallor, rapid improvement supine
Bradykinin angioedema: no itching/hives; ACE inhibitor or hereditary disease → airway, icatibant/C1 inhibitor

anticholinergic-toxicity.name: Anticholinergic toxicity
anticholinergic-toxicity.scope: Antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants, atropine, anticholinergic toxidrome, physostigmine
anticholinergic-toxicity.core: Delirium with mydriasis, dry flushed skin, hyperthermia, urinary retention, and reduced bowel sounds after muscarinic blockade.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Diphenhydramine, first-generation antihistamines in OTC cold/sleep products, atropine, scopolamine, tricyclic antidepressants, toxic plants
Benztropine, trihexyphenidyl for parkinsonism/EPS; chlorpromazine and other low-potency antipsychotics
Older age, polypharmacy, accidental pediatric ingestion, intentional overdose; mixed toxidromes are common

rows.label: Clues
items: Agitation, hallucinations, picking at unseen objects, blurred vision, tachycardia
★ **Hot and dry**, rather than sweaty; severe poisoning causes seizures, coma, dysrhythmias
Palpable bladder, ileus; TCA exposure may add hypotension and conduction abnormalities

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Central/peripheral muscarinic antagonism; some causative drugs also block sodium channels
Absent sweating impairs heat dissipation; agitation further increases temperature
Muscarinic blockade → ↓**detrusor tone** → urinary retention; ↓gut motility → constipation/ileus

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Clinical toxidrome + ECG**; check QRS/QTc before considering reversal
Glucose, electrolytes, creatinine, CK; acetaminophen level for uncertain intentional ingestion
TCA markers: QRS >100 ms or terminal R in aVR signals sodium-channel toxicity
Drug screens do not establish severity; ECG and physiology drive treatment

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Airway support, IV fluids, external cooling; **benzodiazepines** for agitation/seizures
**Stop offending drug** first; bladder catheter for retention; charcoal early only with protected airway
★ Pure severe antimuscarinic delirium → selected **physostigmine**, slow IV with continuous monitoring and expert supervision
Avoid physostigmine with suspected TCA/mixed cardiotoxic ingestion, QRS widening, significant conduction disease, or seizures
Sodium-channel blockade → **IV sodium bicarbonate**; avoid QT-prolonging antipsychotics in high-risk poisoning

rows.label: Complications
items: Rhabdomyolysis, AKI, aspiration, heat injury, ventricular arrhythmia, death
Physostigmine → bradycardia, seizures, asystole in unsuitable patients

rows.label: Prevention
items: Reduce anticholinergic burden, safe storage, avoid duplicate OTC sleep/cold products; assess intent after stabilization

rows.label: Mimics
items: Sympathomimetic toxicity: diaphoresis and active bowel sounds
Serotonin syndrome: clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome: lead-pipe rigidity, dopamine-blocker exposure

anticholinergic-toxicity.evidence: Not checked online; established emergency toxicology teaching.

aortic-dissection.name: Aortic dissection
aortic-dissection.core: Sudden maximal chest or back pain with vascular or neurologic deficits suggests aortic dissection, even without widened mediastinum.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Long-standing hypertension → **medial degeneration** in older adults; bicuspid aortic valve, coarctation
Marfan/vascular Ehlers-Danlos, pregnancy, cocaine, aortic instrumentation or aneurysm

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Abrupt severe pain**, pulse/BP asymmetry, syncope, focal neurologic deficit
New aortic regurgitation murmur; limb ischemia or abdominal pain from branch-vessel malperfusion
Hypotension suggests rupture, tamponade, severe regurgitation, or coronary involvement

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intimal tear → blood separates medial layers, creating false lumen
Propagation compromises branch arteries or ruptures into pericardium/pleura

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Stable → **CTA chest/abdomen/pelvis**; unstable or unable to leave resuscitation → bedside TEE
Chest radiograph may show widened mediastinum but normal film does not exclude dissection
ECG/troponin may mimic MI; high suspicion requires aortic imaging before antithrombotics
Examine bilateral arm pressures, femoral pulses, neurologic status, renal function

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **IV esmolol or labetalol** + opioid analgesia; target HR 60–80 and SBP <120 if perfusion maintained
Persistent hypertension after rate control → nicardipine or nitroprusside; avoid vasodilator before beta blockade
★ **Avoid anticoagulation and thrombolysis** when dissection suspected
Tamponade from dissection → immediate surgical team; routine pericardiocentesis can worsen hemorrhage

rows.label: Complications
items: Aortic rupture, hemothorax, tamponade, MI, stroke, paraplegia, mesenteric/renal ischemia
Late aneurysmal dilation or recurrent dissection despite initial successful treatment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Lifelong **BP control and surveillance CTA/MRA**; beta-blocker-based regimen
Avoid heavy isometric lifting; screen first-degree relatives for familial aortopathy

rows.label: Mimics
items: Acute coronary syndrome: pressure-like pain, no pulse deficit; coexistence possible
PE: pleuritic pain, hypoxemia, right-heart strain
Esophageal rupture: vomiting followed by pain and subcutaneous emphysema

aortic-dissection.evidence: Not checked online; established aortic emergency principles.

appendicitis.name: Appendicitis
appendicitis.scope: Acute appendicitis, clinical presentation, pediatric and pregnancy considerations, imaging (ultrasound, CT), surgical management
appendicitis.core: Periumbilical pain migrating to the right lower quadrant, followed by anorexia and nausea, suggests appendiceal inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Adolescents/young adults; luminal obstruction by lymphoid hyperplasia or fecalith
Older adults may have obstructing neoplasm; immunosuppression can blunt findings

rows.label: Clues
items: McBurney tenderness, guarding, fever; Rovsing, psoas, or obturator signs depend on position
★ **Diffuse peritonitis, toxicity, hypotension** → perforation/sepsis until proven otherwise
Young children: nonspecific symptoms and rapid progression; pregnancy: displaced appendix, less reliable examination

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal obstruction → distention, venous congestion, bacterial invasion → ischemia/perforation
Visceral midgut pain precedes focal parietal peritoneal irritation

rows.label: Dx
items: CBC, urinalysis, **pregnancy test** in reproductive-age patients; pyuria does not exclude appendicitis
★ Stable nonpregnant adult → **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** when diagnosis uncertain
★ Child/pregnancy → **ultrasound first**; nondiagnostic → MRI without gadolinium, or CT in nonpregnant child
Noncompressible enlarged appendix >6 mm with periappendiceal inflammation supports diagnosis
Clear peritonitis → surgical evaluation; do not delay necessary operation for repeated imaging

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ NPO, **IV fluids, IV opioids, ceftriaxone + metronidazole**, surgical consultation; opioids do not obscure exam
Laparoscopic appendectomy definitive; do not withhold necessary surgery during pregnancy
Selected uncomplicated cases → antibiotics after shared decision; recurrence/failure higher, especially with appendicolith
Localized abscess/phlegmon in stable patient → antibiotics ± image-guided drainage; follow-up based on age/risk

rows.label: Complications
items: Perforation, abscess, peritonitis, sepsis, ileus
Postoperative wound infection, intra-abdominal collection, adhesional obstruction

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, adnexal findings
Ovarian torsion: sudden unilateral pelvic pain; gastroenteritis: diarrhea prominent before diffuse cramping
Mesenteric adenitis: viral prodrome, normal appendix on imaging

appendicitis.evidence: Not checked online; established general-surgery evaluation and treatment principles.

asthma.name: Asthma
asthma.scope: Diagnosis, stepwise therapy, acute exacerbation, exercise-induced bronchoconstriction
asthma.core: Variable episodes of wheeze, cough, dyspnea, and chest tightness from reversible expiratory airflow limitation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: **Family history of asthma/atopy**: strongest childhood risk; allergens, viral infections, smoke, occupational sensitizers
Exercise/cold air, aspirin-sensitive disease, nonselective beta-blockers; assess workplace symptom pattern

rows.label: Clues
items: Nocturnal/early-morning symptoms; normal examination between attacks
★ **Silent chest, exhaustion, altered mentation, rising PaCO2** → impending respiratory failure
Acute attack: low peak flow, accessory-muscle use, difficulty speaking
Cough-variant: isolated chronic cough, worse with cold/exercise; normal examination and radiograph

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Allergen cross-links IgE on **mast cells** → histamine, leukotrienes → bronchoconstriction
Airway inflammation, smooth-muscle constriction, mucus → variable obstruction and hyperresponsiveness
Persistent uncontrolled inflammation → remodeling with incompletely reversible airflow limitation

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Spirometry**: obstruction with bronchodilator FEV1 increase >12% and >200 mL in adults
Normal spirometry with suspicion → repeat during symptoms or methacholine challenge
Exercise challenge: postexercise FEV1 fall >10%; assess baseline control before isolated exercise diagnosis
PFT pattern: ↓FEV1, normal/↓FVC, normal/↑TLC from air trapping

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Exacerbation → **repeated inhaled albuterol + ipratropium**, oxygen, early systemic glucocorticoids
Severe poor response → IV magnesium; deterioration → intubation; avoid sedatives and routine antibiotics
Exercise symptoms → preexercise albuterol or prescribed ICS-formoterol; persistent symptoms → improve controller
Check technique/adherence before stepping up; uncontrolled despite high-dose ICS-LABA → phenotype-directed biologic referral
Discharge: **PEF ≥70–80% predicted** (less wheeze is unreliable) + 5–7 day **oral prednisone** prevents relapse

rows.label: Complications
items: Status asthmaticus, pneumothorax, respiratory arrest
ICS → thrush/dysphonia; systemic steroids → osteoporosis, hyperglycemia, adrenal suppression

rows.label: Prevention
items: Written action plan, trigger reduction, smoking cessation, spacer; rinse mouth after ICS
★ GINA: **no SABA-only treatment**, no LABA monotherapy; ICS with every reliever use
Older exam questions (NAEPP) may expect: symptoms ≤2 days/week, awakenings ≤2/month → **SABA alone**; more → daily ICS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Inducible laryngeal obstruction: inspiratory stridor, inspiratory flow-loop flattening
COPD: persistent obstruction, smoking history
HF: edema, elevated JVP, cardiac findings
Deconditioning: obese/sedentary, exertional dyspnea; normal PFTs, no bronchodilator response

bite-wounds.name: Bite wounds
bite-wounds.scope: Cat bites (Pasteurella multocida), dog bites, human bites (Eikenella corrodens), wound irrigation, closure vs secondary intention, amoxicillin-clavulanate, rabies and tetanus prophylaxis
bite-wounds.core: Animal or human bites combine tissue damage with polymicrobial inoculation; hand injuries and deep punctures carry disproportionate infection risk.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Cat punctures, delayed presentation, diabetes, immunosuppression, asplenia, wounds near joints
Clenched-fist injury over MCP joint → occult human bite with possible tendon penetration

rows.label: Clues
items: Rapid pain, erythema, swelling, drainage; infection may appear within hours after a cat bite
★ Pain with passive movement, restricted motion, systemic toxicity → **deep-space infection**

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mixed aerobes/anaerobes introduced below skin; narrow punctures trap organisms
Crush injury and devitalized tissue impair clearance; tendon sheaths permit proximal spread

rows.label: Dx
items: Neurovascular/tendon examination; assess joint penetration and retained foreign material
Radiograph for hand fight bite, suspected tooth fragment, bone injury, or osteomyelitis
Culture infected drainage; no routine culture of an uninfected fresh wound

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Copious irrigation + debridement**; hand elevation, assess need for surgical exploration
★ Human/cat/hand bite prophylaxis or infection → **amoxicillin-clavulanate**; severe → IV ampicillin-sulbactam
Prophylaxis usually 3–5 days; established infection needs longer, guided by depth and response
★ Hand or human bites, punctures, infected wounds → **leave open**; clean facial lacerations → primary closure
Rabies-risk exposure: unvaccinated → wound HRIG + vaccine days 0, 3, 7, 14; immunocompromised add 28

rows.label: Complications
items: Tenosynovitis, septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, bacteremia; asplenia → fulminant Capnocytophaga sepsis
Rabies almost universally fatal after symptoms begin

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Dirty wound: **tetanus booster if ≥5 years**; unknown/incomplete series → vaccine + TIG
Prior rabies vaccination → vaccine days 0, 3; no HRIG; public health assesses animal risk
Healthy dog/cat/ferret available → 10-day observation coordinated with public health; animal-handling education

rows.label: Mimics
items: Nonbite cellulitis: no inoculation history or puncture
Crystal arthritis: joint inflammation with crystals, but aspiration still needed if infection possible

table.title: Characteristic pathogens
rows: Eikenella corrodens; mixed oral/skin flora, anaerobes

bowel-obstruction.name: Bowel obstruction
bowel-obstruction.scope: Small bowel obstruction (adhesions, hernia), large bowel obstruction (volvulus, malignancy), paralytic ileus, NG decompression, surgical management
bowel-obstruction.core: Colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, distention, and obstipation suggest mechanical obstruction; constant pain or systemic toxicity raises concern for strangulation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior abdominal surgery (**adhesions**, leading cause), incarcerated hernia, Crohn strictures → small-bowel obstruction
Colorectal malignancy, chronic constipation, institutionalization → large-bowel obstruction or sigmoid volvulus
Recent surgery, opioids, hypokalemia, severe systemic illness → ileus

rows.label: Clues
items: Early high-pitched sounds may become absent; proximal obstruction causes earlier vomiting, distal disease greater distention
★ **Peritonitis, fever, tachycardia, rising lactate**, or continuous severe pain → ischemia/perforation
Complete → **obstipation**, no flatus; partial may still pass stool/diarrhea, not excluding obstruction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Luminal blockage → upstream dilation, third spacing; closed loop compromises venous then arterial supply
Adynamic ileus reflects impaired motility without an anatomic transition point

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast** defines transition point, cause, and ischemic signs
CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, lactate; normal lactate cannot exclude early ischemia
Radiograph may show dilated loops/air-fluid levels, no rectal gas; CT more definitive if diagnosis uncertain
★ Massive colonic distention + **coffee-bean (inverted-U) loop** on radiograph → sigmoid volvulus
Pregnancy: plain radiograph acceptable first (minimal fetal dose); MRI if unclear; do not delay

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **NPO, IV isotonic fluids, electrolyte correction**; NG decompression for significant vomiting/distention
★ Strangulation, perforation, closed loop, or incarcerated hernia → **urgent surgery** + ceftriaxone/metronidazole
Uncomplicated adhesive SBO → surgical observation, serial examination; water-soluble contrast helps predict resolution
Failure to improve during a short monitored trial, commonly up to 72 h → operation
Ileus → correct trigger, reduce opioids, mobilize; no operation solely for absent sounds

rows.label: Complications
items: Dehydration, AKI, hypokalemic alkalosis; bowel necrosis, perforation, sepsis
Recurrent adhesions; short-bowel syndrome after extensive resection

rows.label: Prevention
items: Early postoperative ambulation, opioid-sparing analgesia, electrolyte correction; elective repair of symptomatic hernias

rows.label: Mimics
items: Gastroenteritis: prominent diarrhea, no focal transition point
Mesenteric ischemia: pain out of proportion before peritoneal signs
Ileus: hypoactive/absent sounds, gas throughout bowel including rectum
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy: dysmotility, dilated loops without transition point

table.title: Large-bowel branches
rows: Sigmoidoscopic detorsion, rectal tube → same-admission resection

bowel-obstruction.evidence: Not checked online; established acute surgical management principles.

carbon-monoxide-poisoning.name: Carbon monoxide poisoning
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.scope: Carboxyhemoglobin, pulse oximetry pitfall, normobaric and hyperbaric oxygen indications, delayed neurologic sequelae
carbon-monoxide-poisoning.core: Headache, dizziness, nausea, or confusion affecting several people in an enclosed combustion setting suggests carbon monoxide exposure.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: House fires, faulty heaters, generators indoors, vehicle exhaust, poorly ventilated fuel-burning equipment
Pregnancy, infancy, anemia, and cardiopulmonary disease increase vulnerability at a given exposure

rows.label: Clues
items: Odorless gas: flulike illness without fever; symptoms improve outside exposure site
★ **Syncope, altered consciousness, focal deficits, chest pain**, or severe acidosis → serious toxicity
**Cherry-red/flushed skin, pink mucosa** + indoor coma → suspect CO; often absent, normal color not reassuring

rows.label: Pathophys
items: CO binds hemoglobin avidly, reduces oxygen carriage, shifts dissociation curve left
Mitochondrial dysfunction and inflammation add tissue injury; fetal hemoglobin retains CO longer

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Venous or arterial co-oximetry** measures carboxyhemoglobin; draw promptly without delaying oxygen
★ **Normal pulse oximetry and PaO₂ do not exclude poisoning**; both can appear reassuring
COHb >2% in nonsmokers or >9% in smokers supports exposure; level poorly predicts outcome
ECG, troponin for cardiac injury; lactate/ABG for acidosis; pregnancy testing when relevant
Prior oxygen or delayed presentation lowers COHb; exposure history remains decisive

rows.label: Tx
items: Remove from source, protect rescuers, assess airway and ventilation
★ **100% oxygen by nonrebreather** immediately; intubate for coma or respiratory failure
Consider hyperbaric oxygen for neurologic impairment, loss of consciousness, cardiac injury, severe acidosis, or COHb >25–30%
Pregnancy → urgent hyperbaric consultation at lower severity/levels; treatment decisions integrate symptoms, not COHb alone
Smoke inhalation + profound lactic acidosis/shock → consider cyanide, give hydroxocobalamin

rows.label: Complications
items: Myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, death; delayed cognitive, behavioral, gait, or movement deficits after recovery
Follow-up for delayed neurologic symptoms; mild initial presentation does not exclude later deficits

rows.label: Prevention
items: Working CO detectors, professional heater inspection, never run generators or engines indoors
Public safety evaluation before returning to the exposure site

rows.label: Mimics
items: Viral illness: fever and infectious contacts rather than shared building exposure
Methemoglobinemia: cyanosis, saturation near 85%, chocolate-colored blood
Cyanide poisoning: rapid collapse, marked lactate elevation after enclosed fire

cervical-artery-dissection.name: Cervical artery dissection
cervical-artery-dissection.scope: Carotid artery dissection, vertebral artery dissection, Horner syndrome, posterior circulation stroke, imaging, antithrombotic therapy
cervical-artery-dissection.core: Young or middle-aged adult with sudden unilateral head or neck pain followed by retinal or cerebral ischemia after minor neck trauma.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Neck manipulation, hyperextension, sporting injury, coughing; spontaneous cases common
Fibromuscular dysplasia, connective-tissue disorders, migraine, recent infection

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Painful partial Horner syndrome**: ptosis + miosis, often without facial anhidrosis
Carotid: monocular visual loss, aphasia, contralateral weakness; pulsatile tinnitus possible
Vertebral: occipital pain, ataxia, vertigo; **lateral medullary syndrome** (crossed sensory loss, hoarseness, Horner)
Pain may precede ischemia by hours or days; normal initial neurologic examination does not exclude dissection

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Intimal tear or vasa vasorum hemorrhage → intramural hematoma and arterial narrowing
Mural thrombus embolization usually causes stroke; expansion may compress adjacent sympathetic fibers

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CTA head and neck** rapidly evaluates carotid/vertebral lumen and associated occlusion
MRA with fat-suppressed neck MRI identifies mural hematoma; brain MRI detects infarction
Tapered stenosis, intimal flap, pseudoaneurysm support diagnosis; catheter angiography for equivocal/interventional cases
Do not rely on carotid ultrasound alone for distal carotid or vertebral lesions

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Eligible acute ischemic stroke → **IV thrombolysis and/or thrombectomy**; dissection alone is no exclusion
★ Extracranial dissection → **antiplatelet or anticoagulation for 3–6 months**, individualized bleeding/ischemic risk
Repeat vascular imaging guides follow-up; no proven universal superiority of anticoagulation
Recurrent ischemia despite medical treatment or critical hemodynamic compromise → specialist consideration of stenting
Intracranial extension/subarachnoid hemorrhage → urgent neurovascular consultation; avoid reflex anticoagulation

rows.label: Complications
items: TIA, retinal infarction, ischemic stroke, dissecting pseudoaneurysm
Intracranial dissections may rupture into subarachnoid space; recurrent extracranial events uncommon

rows.label: Prevention
items: Avoid neck manipulation/contact injury while healing; control vascular risks
High-risk connective-tissue disease → individualized long-term activity counseling

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cluster headache: episodic autonomic headache without persistent ischemic findings
Pancoast tumor: gradual Horner syndrome with shoulder/arm symptoms
BPPV: brief positional vertigo without focal deficits or acute neck pain

cervicitis-pid.name: Cervicitis and pelvic inflammatory disease
cervicitis-pid.core: Sexually active patient with mucopurulent discharge or postcoital bleeding; ascending infection adds pelvic pain, sometimes an adnexal abscess.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age <25 (adolescent cervical ectopy → vulnerable columnar epithelium), new/multiple partners, inconsistent condoms, prior STI
IUD-associated PID risk concentrated within first 3 weeks after insertion

rows.label: Clues
items: Cervical friability, easily induced endocervical bleeding; infection sometimes asymptomatic
Dyspareunia, fever; severe unilateral pain/adnexal mass → **tubo-ovarian abscess**
Peritonitis, shock → rupture; RUQ pain → Fitz-Hugh–Curtis perihepatitis
Persistent dysuria, sterile pyuria, negative culture → chlamydial urethritis, not UTI

rows.label: Pathophys
items: GC/CT ascend cervix → endometrium/tubes; PID often polymicrobial, including anaerobes
Chlamydial tubal damage: **host immune response** → scarring, hydrosalpinx

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test** first; vaginal/cervical or urine **GC/CT NAAT**; HIV/syphilis testing
★ Pelvic pain + **cervical motion, uterine, OR adnexal tenderness** → presumptive PID; no confirmation delay
Negative cervical NAAT does not exclude upper-tract infection; normal discharge/no vaginal leukocytes argues against PID
**Transvaginal US** for abscess or diagnostic uncertainty; routine laparoscopy unnecessary

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Cervicitis: empiric GC/CT coverage IF high risk/unreliable follow-up; otherwise await NAAT
★ Admit IF **pregnant, abscess, severe illness**, oral intolerance, uncertain surgical diagnosis, or failure by 72 h
Abscess rupture → emergency surgery; persistent abscess after 48–72 h antibiotics → drainage
Pregnant chlamydia → **azithromycin**, avoid doxycycline; retain IUD initially, reassess if no improvement

rows.label: Complications
items: Tubal infertility, ectopic pregnancy, chronic pelvic pain; abscess → sepsis

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Treat partners from prior **60 days**; abstain until courses completed, partners treated, symptoms resolved
Retest GC/CT at 3 months; pregnant chlamydia → test of cure at 4 weeks
Annual GC/CT screening: sexually active women <25, older women with risks; condoms

rows.label: Mimics
items: Ectopic pregnancy: positive hCG, no confirmed intrauterine pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt unilateral pain, vomiting; Doppler flow may persist
Appendicitis: migrating RLQ pain, CT appendiceal inflammation

table.title: Antibiotic branches
rows: Ceftriaxone; add CT regimen unless excluded
Oral drugs 14 days; ceftriaxone once IM outpatient

delirium.name: Delirium
delirium.scope: Diagnostic criteria, precipitating causes (infection, metabolic, drugs), workup, management and prevention
delirium.core: Acute fluctuating inattention with altered cognition or awareness indicates delirium and requires a search for physiologic triggers.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Older age, baseline dementia, frailty, sensory impairment, hospitalization or recent surgery
Infection (UTI, pneumonia, wound), hypoxia, metabolic derangement, dehydration, retention, constipation and uncontrolled pain
Anticholinergics (amitriptyline), meperidine, other opioids, steroids, sedatives; alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal

rows.label: Clues
items: Disorganized thinking, sleep–wake reversal, hallucinations; hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed presentation
★ Hypoactive withdrawal/lethargy easily missed; **test attention**, not orientation alone
Digit span, months backward or inability to sustain conversation reveals attentional deficit
**Asterixis** → toxic-metabolic encephalopathy of any cause, not only hepatic failure

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Systemic stress and drug effects disrupt vulnerable brain networks and neurotransmitter balance
Multiple small precipitating factors can exceed low cognitive reserve

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **CAM**: acute/fluctuating course + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness
Immediate glucose, oxygenation, vitals; focused neurologic examination, medication review and collateral baseline
CBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function; ECG, chest imaging guided by findings; wound/sepsis signs → **blood cultures**
CT head for focal deficit, trauma or unexplained reduced consciousness; LP for suspected CNS infection
Fever, urinary symptoms or dementia → **urinalysis** for UTI before CT/LP; bacteriuria alone doesn't prove cause

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ **Treat precipitant**; reorient, restore hearing/glasses, hydrate, mobilize and normalize sleep
Calm environment and familiar support; remove unnecessary catheters and avoid physical restraints
★ Severe distress or danger despite de-escalation → short course **haloperidol**, check QT/EPS risk
Parkinson disease/Lewy body dementia → avoid potent dopamine blockers; specialist-guided alternative
Benzodiazepines generally worsen delirium; reserve for withdrawal or selected seizures/catatonia

rows.label: Complications
items: Falls, aspiration, prolonged hospitalization, functional decline, persistent cognitive impairment and increased mortality
Antipsychotics may prolong QT; sedation may conceal clinical deterioration

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Multicomponent prevention: orientation, daytime activity, sleep protection, hydration, pain control and drug review
Minimize nighttime interruptions and unnecessary sedatives; encourage family engagement

rows.label: Mimics
items: Dementia: chronic progression; attention relatively preserved early
Depression: sustained mood symptoms without fluctuating consciousness
Primary psychosis: usually preserved attention and alertness

drowning-and-submersion-injury.name: Drowning and submersion injury
drowning-and-submersion-injury.scope: Submersion injury, nonfatal drowning, hypoxemia, acute lung injury/ARDS, electrolyte disturbances, observation criteria
drowning-and-submersion-injury.core: Respiratory impairment from submersion causes hypoxemia; prompt ventilation is the central lifesaving intervention.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Unsupervised children, absent barriers/life jackets, alcohol, seizures, syncope, risky water activity
Cold water, prolonged submersion, delayed rescue, underlying cardiac channelopathy worsen risk

rows.label: Clues
items: Cough, dyspnea, crackles, frothy sputum, hypothermia, altered consciousness
★ **Persistent hypoxemia or respiratory distress** predicts evolving lung injury despite initially mild examination
Freshwater versus saltwater rarely changes clinical management

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Aspiration washes out surfactant and injures alveoli → noncardiogenic edema, intrapulmonary shunt
Systemic oxygen deprivation causes bradycardia, cardiac arrest, and neurologic injury

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Assess **oxygenation, breathing, temperature, mental status** immediately
ABG/electrolytes for severe injury; chest radiograph for respiratory symptoms, not mandatory in completely well patients
Evaluate trauma, intoxication, arrhythmia, seizure, or hypoglycemia as precipitating cause
Early normal radiograph does not guarantee normal subsequent respiratory course

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Safe rescue → **rescue breaths plus CPR** if arrest; oxygen/BVM for inadequate respirations
Intubate for refractory hypoxemia, severe fatigue, or absent airway protection; lung-protective ventilation with PEEP
Remove wet clothing, rewarm; immobilize cervical spine only when mechanism suggests injury
★ No routine **antibiotics or corticosteroids**; antibiotics for infection or grossly contaminated-water exposure
Observe mild cases 4–6 hours; admit for abnormal mentation, oxygen requirement, persistent symptoms, or deterioration

rows.label: Complications
items: ARDS, hypoxic brain injury, pneumonia, arrhythmia, multiorgan dysfunction
Pulmonary edema may evolve over hours; asymptomatic wellness for days does not predict sudden delayed drowning
Massive freshwater aspiration → **dilutional hyponatremia**, seizures; rare currently, older exam questions may expect it

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ **Four-sided pool fencing**, touch supervision, swim lessons, properly fitted life jackets
Avoid alcohol and swimming alone; seizure precautions; caregivers trained in ventilation-inclusive CPR

rows.label: Mimics
items: Cardiogenic edema: primary cardiac disease, elevated filling pressures
Immersion pulmonary edema: swimming-associated dyspnea without submersion/aspiration
Aspiration pneumonitis: gastric contents after vomiting rather than water exposure

ectopic-pregnancy.name: Ectopic pregnancy
ectopic-pregnancy.scope: Diagnosis (beta-hCG, transvaginal ultrasound, discriminatory zone), unruptured ectopic pregnancy, medical management (methotrexate), ruptured ectopic pregnancy, surgical management
ectopic-pregnancy.core: Pregnancy implanted outside the endometrial cavity, usually tubal; early pregnancy with pelvic pain or bleeding requires localization and rupture assessment.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Prior ectopic, PID/tubal damage, tubal surgery, infertility treatment, smoking
IUDs prevent pregnancy overall; pregnancy despite IUD has higher ectopic proportion; many cases lack risks

rows.label: Clues
items: Amenorrhea, unilateral pelvic pain, spotting; cervical motion/adnexal tenderness nonspecific
★ **Syncope, shoulder-tip pain, peritoneal signs, hypotension** → hemoperitoneum/rupture
Heterotopic pregnancy possible despite visualized intrauterine pregnancy, particularly after assisted reproduction

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Impaired tubal transport → extrauterine trophoblastic implantation, invasion, hemorrhage
Methotrexate inhibits folate-dependent DNA synthesis in proliferating trophoblast

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Pregnancy test → quantitative beta-hCG + transvaginal ultrasound**; ultrasound regardless of hCG when symptomatic
Extrauterine yolk sac/embryo diagnostic; adnexal mass/free fluid supportive; empty uterus alone insufficient
★ Stable pregnancy of unknown location → **repeat hCG in 48 hours**, serial ultrasound until resolved/localized
Subnormal 48-hour hCG rise + empty uterus + pain → suspect **ectopic**; rapid fall favors miscarriage
Discriminatory threshold up to 3,500 mIU/mL protects viable IUP; abnormal rise/fall cannot establish location

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Unstable/rupture concern → **IV access, blood resuscitation, urgent laparotomy**; do not await serial hCG
Confirmed unruptured, stable, reliable follow-up, hCG <5,000, mass <3.5 cm, no fetal heartbeat → consider **methotrexate**
Avoid methotrexate: viable IUP, breastfeeding, hepatic/renal disease, cytopenias, immunodeficiency, unreliable follow-up
Postmethotrexate hCG days 4/7: fall ≥15% → weekly until negative; inadequate fall → reassess/re-dose/surgery

rows.label: Complications
items: Hemorrhagic shock, death, tubal loss, recurrence, impaired fertility
Methotrexate: mucositis, hepatotoxicity, marrow suppression; rupture remains possible despite falling hCG

rows.label: Prevention
items: Treat/prevent STIs, smoking cessation; prior ectopic → early ultrasound in subsequent pregnancy
Methotrexate counseling: avoid alcohol, folate supplements, intercourse until resolution; avoid conception for 3 months
Unsensitized Rh-negative ectopic → Rh(D) immune globulin; provide return precautions for escalating pain/dizziness

rows.label: Mimics
items: Miscarriage: intrauterine pregnancy loss; passage of decidual tissue alone does not prove IUP
Hemorrhagic corpus luteum: ovarian source, may coexist with normal pregnancy
Ovarian torsion: abrupt severe unilateral pain, enlarged ovary

table.title: Alternative definitive branches
rows: Stable, minimal symptoms, low declining hCG
Selected expectant management with reliable surveillance
Heartbeat, high hCG, severe pain, or contraindication

ectopic-pregnancy.evidence: Checked 2026-10-30: [ACOG ectopic pregnancy](https://www.acog.org/womens-health/faqs/ectopic-pregnancy), [NICE tubal ectopic management](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/NG126/chapter/management-of-tubal-ectopic-pregnancy); conservative discriminatory threshold established ACOG teaching.

febrile-seizures.name: Febrile seizures
febrile-seizures.scope: Simple febrile seizures, complex febrile seizures, diagnostic evaluation, antipyretics and reassurance, recurrence risk
febrile-seizures.core: Seizure during fever in a child aged 6–60 months, without CNS infection, metabolic cause, or prior afebrile seizures.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Young age, family history, viral febrile illness; often occurs early in illness
Recurrence more likely with first episode <18 months, lower fever, brief preceding fever, affected relative

rows.label: Clues
items: Transient postictal sleepiness followed by return to baseline; normal neurologic examination between events
★ **Meningismus, persistent altered mental status, toxic appearance**, or focal deficit → alternate urgent diagnosis

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Age-dependent neuronal excitability lowers seizure threshold during inflammatory illness
Not caused by a particular temperature rise rate; fever can be recognized only after seizure

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ Typical simple event → **clinical diagnosis; evaluate fever source**, not routine EEG or brain imaging
Bedside glucose for ongoing seizure, prolonged altered state, or concerning metabolic context
★ Suspected meningitis → **LP**; consider at 6–12 months with incomplete Hib/pneumococcal immunization
Prior antibiotics may mask meningitis; complex features prompt individualized neurologic/CNS infection evaluation
No routine electrolyte panel after brief event with normal recovery and hydration

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Ongoing seizure **>5 minutes → benzodiazepine**, airway positioning, oxygen, glucose assessment
Stopped seizure, well child → reassurance, hydration, identify and treat fever source
Acetaminophen or ibuprofen improves comfort; antipyretics do not reliably prevent future febrile seizures
No chronic phenobarbital or valproate for simple events; harms exceed preventive benefit

rows.label: Complications
items: Approximately one-third recur; simple episodes do not cause intellectual disability or brain damage
Later epilepsy risk low after simple events; higher with complex features or abnormal neurodevelopment

rows.label: Prevention
items: ★ Parent plan: **side positioning, time event, nothing in mouth**; emergency help for prolonged seizure
Selected recurrent prolonged events → home rescue intranasal midazolam or rectal diazepam plan

rows.label: Mimics
items: Meningitis: sustained encephalopathy, meningeal signs, CSF inflammation
Rigors: preserved consciousness during shivering
Epilepsy: unprovoked events outside febrile illness

febrile-seizures.evidence: Not checked online; established pediatric febrile seizure evaluation principles.

gallstone-disease.name: Gallstone disease
gallstone-disease.scope: Biliary colic, acute cholecystitis, choledocholithiasis, cholangitis, gallstone pancreatitis
gallstone-disease.core: Gallstone location determines the syndrome: transient cystic obstruction, gallbladder inflammation, common-duct obstruction/infection, or pancreatic inflammation.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: Age, female sex, pregnancy, obesity, rapid weight loss, ileal disease/resection
Hemolysis/cirrhosis → pigment stones; critical illness/TPN → acalculous cholecystitis

rows.label: Clues
items: Postprandial RUQ/epigastric discomfort radiating to back or right shoulder; assess fever and jaundice
★ **Fever + RUQ pain + jaundice** → cholangitis; hypotension/confusion → severe infection
Pancreatitis: persistent epigastric pain radiating to back, vomiting; ALT >150 supports biliary cause

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Cholesterol supersaturation or pigment precipitation creates calculi; obstruction location dictates organ injury
Infected obstructed bile ducts require drainage because antibiotics cannot reliably sterilize a closed system

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **RUQ ultrasound first**; CBC, bilirubin/alkaline phosphatase, AST/ALT, lipase
Suspected cholecystitis with equivocal ultrasound → HIDA; nonvisualized gallbladder supports cystic-duct obstruction
Intermediate common-duct stone probability → MRCP or EUS; ERCP reserved primarily for treatment
★ Direct intervention: **stone seen, cholangitis, or bilirubin >4 mg/dL plus dilated duct**
Post-cholecystectomy jaundice + dilated ducts → retained stone/duct injury → **ERCP**; HIDA only for bile leak

rows.label: Tx
items: Analgesia, fluids, antiemetics; infection → ceftriaxone/metronidazole or piperacillin/tazobactam
★ **Cholangitis → urgent biliary drainage**, immediately after stabilization if shock; do not await antibiotic response
Poor surgical candidate with acute cholecystitis → percutaneous cholecystostomy
★ Gallstone pancreatitis → supportive care, early oral feeding; **no urgent ERCP without cholangitis/persistent obstruction**

rows.label: Complications
items: Empyema, gangrene, perforation, abscess, septic shock; pancreatitis → necrosis/organ failure
Cholecystoenteric fistula → gallstone ileus; imaging: bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, ectopic stone
ERCP → pancreatitis/bleeding/perforation

rows.label: Prevention
items: Maintain healthy weight; avoid rapid weight loss; selected bariatric patients → ursodiol prophylaxis
After duct clearance → cholecystectomy; after mild biliary pancreatitis → same-admission cholecystectomy
Asymptomatic uncomplicated stones → observation; no routine prophylactic surgery

rows.label: Mimics
items: Hepatitis: marked aminotransferase elevation, no obstructing stone
PUD: burning epigastric pain, ulcer on endoscopy
Inferior MI: ischemic ECG/troponin changes, cardiovascular risk

table.title: Localizing obstruction
rows: Persistent >6 hours, Murphy sign, wall thickening
Cholestatic labs, duct stone/dilation; no infection
ERCP extraction or operative duct clearance
Inflamed gallbladder without stones; critically ill

gastrointestinal-bleeding.name: Gastrointestinal bleeding
gastrointestinal-bleeding.scope: Upper GI bleeding (PUD, varices, Mallory-Weiss), lower GI bleeding (diverticular, angiodysplasia, hemorrhoids), fluid and transfusion thresholds, endoscopy
gastrointestinal-bleeding.core: Hematemesis, melena, or hematochezia → assess hemodynamics before localizing; brisk upper bleeding can present as bright red rectal blood.

rows.label: Risk factors
items: NSAIDs/H pylori → ulcers; cirrhosis → varices; forceful retching → mucosal tear
Anticoagulants/antiplatelets increase severity; older age favors diverticula or angiodysplasia

rows.label: Clues
items: ★ **Syncope, orthostasis, shock** signal major loss; initial hemoglobin may remain normal
Epigastric pain supports ulcer; painless bleeding favors vascular sources
Recurrent occult loss → iron deficiency
**Melena**, elevated BUN/creatinine ratio → upper source; bilious NG aspirate argues against upper bleeding

rows.label: Pathophys
items: Mucosal injury, portal-pressure collaterals, or fragile vessels rupture into GI lumen
Volume depletion → reduced perfusion; ongoing bleeding may require massive transfusion

rows.label: Dx
items: ★ **Two large-bore IVs, CBC, type/cross, coagulation tests**, serial hemoglobin; resuscitate before procedures
Upper source → EGD within 24 hours after stabilization; suspected varices → within 12 hours
★ Ongoing hemodynamically significant hematochezia → **CT angiography → embolization** if active extravasation
Stable lower bleeding → bowel preparation and nonemergent colonoscopy; routine <24-hour colonoscopy adds no benefit
Rectal bleeding mixed with stool, age ≥45 → colonoscopy; negative FOBT does not exclude neoplasia

rows.label: Tx
items: ★ Crystalloid initially; stable nonischemic adults → **RBC transfusion at hemoglobin <7 g/dL**
Exsanguination or post-crystalloid shock → **RBCs** regardless of hemoglobin, not vasopressors; cardiac ischemia → higher threshold
Severe anticoagulant bleeding → drug-specific reversal; uncontrolled varices → balloon tamponade as temporary bridge only
Failed endoscopy → IR/surgery; massive unlocalized lower bleeding → **total abdominal colectomy**, not segmental
Suspected ulcer → IV PPI; endoscopic hemostasis for active bleeding/visible vessel, then high-dose PPI

rows.label: Complications
items: Rebleeding, aspiration, myocardial ischemia, AKI; variceal bleeding → infection
Massive transfusion → hypocalcemia, hypothermia, coagulopathy; embolization → bowel ischemia

rows.label: Prevention
items: Eradicate H pylori and confirm cure; avoid NSAIDs; PPI for high-risk users
After variceal control: nonselective beta-blocker plus repeat banding; recurrent bleeding → TIPS

rows.label: Mimics
items: Iron/bismuth: dark stool without blood loss
Hemoptysis: coughing frothy blood rather than vomiting
Swallowed epistaxis: nasal source on examination

rows: Postretching tear; Boerhaave instead: chest pain, crepitus
Liver trauma + jaundice; blood from ampulla
